subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Tea on the Silk Road
description: A short lesson to help you apply Tea on the Silk Road.

hook.text: Tea bricks were so valuable on the Silk Road that they served as currency in Tibet and Mongolia.

buildup.text: Compressed tea survived months of caravan travel. Loose leaves would have spoiled or blown away.

discovery.text: The Tea Horse Road linked China's Yunnan province to Tibet—traders swapped tea for Tibetan warhorses.

twist.text: Tibetans mixed tea with yak butter and salt. They drank up to 40 cups daily for calories at high altitude.

climax.text: These trade routes shaped alliances, economies, and cultures across Central Asia for over a thousand years.

punchline.text: Bricks of tea bought warhorses. Caffeine was currency.

quiz.question: What was the Tea Horse Road?
options: A trade route swapping tea for Tibetan warhorses

details.summary: Tea traveled along the ancient Silk Road and the Tea Horse Road from China to Central Asia, Tibet, Mongolia, and eventually Russia. Compressed tea bricks served as both a trade good and a form of currency. Tea became essential to the nomadic diets of steppe peoples as a source of vitamins.
details.whyItMatters: The Silk Road spread tea across Asia, making it one of history's most consequential traded goods and connecting civilizations through a shared beverage culture.
takeaways: Tea traveled the Silk Road from China to Central and Western Asia
Compressed tea bricks doubled as currency in border trade
Nomadic peoples adopted tea as a vital dietary supplement

faq.question: What was the Tea Horse Road?
faq.answer: The Tea Horse Road was an ancient trade route connecting tea-producing regions of Yunnan and Sichuan with Tibet and beyond. Chinese tea was exchanged for Tibetan war horses. The route traversed some of the world's most challenging mountain terrain and operated for over a thousand years.

faq.question: Why were tea bricks used as currency?
faq.answer: Compressed tea bricks were durable, portable, universally valued, and could be broken into smaller pieces for transactions. In regions where coins were scarce, tea bricks served as a reliable medium of exchange. Their value was based on weight and quality.
